01-feature-building.notes: All five pass the hidden 11-test contract suite and my 20,000-graph brute-force fuzz, including the cyclic/acyclic decision. The differences are in cycle diagnostics, robustness and tests. Most cross-test failures are stricter than the contract: exact message wording (A's regexes vs E's quoted IDs), extra validation the brief never asked for (non-Job items, priority type, bare-string depends_on), and C's split on ';'. I did not count these against contract correctness. The one cross-test failure that exposes a real contract bug is B's RecursionError on long cycles (A's and E's suites). D's cycle message counts as 'including the IDs involved', but it mislabels downstream jobs, so I took off a little. C's float rejection is defensible given 'priority: int'. Its double read of depends_on only affects one-shot iterables (outside the type annotation), so the deduction is small. Mutants were applied by wrapping each submission's own implementation, which keeps each suite's message-wording assertions intact. There were 20 behavioural mutants: wrong tie-breaks (reverse, by id, FIFO by readiness), ascending priority, level-by-level scheduling, no priority, empty input -> None, generator dropped, skipped dup/empty/non-string/unknown checks, duplicate deps stalling, cycle errors without IDs / silent / RecursionError / all IDs, mutated depends_on, dropped or duplicated output. Kill counts: A 20, C 19, E 19, D 15, B 14. A and E are close; A edges ahead on a full mutant kill and a reference-comparison property test inside the suite.

B's choice to purge in __len__ is allowed and not penalized as behavior, but the test that fails every other correct submission costs B 0.25 on regression coverage. C's and D's len()==0-after-expired-get tests are also slightly beyond the brief, but they do not fail any submission and were not penalized. Regression coverage was measured against 9 original-bug mutants plus 4 extras. C and D catch all 13. B catches all 13 once its own len test is excluded. E catches all 9 original bugs but misses purge-front-only. A misses 2 of the 9 original bugs (put-update recency, purge-before-evict) despite claiming to cover them. C and D tie at 10; D is ranked first for its slightly broader boundary and falsy-expiry cases. B and E tie at 9.75; B is ranked higher because it catches strictly more mutants.

opus-5.5.summary: The most careful and complete guide. It has a three-way Guarantee/Recommendation/Unconfirmed legend, a header table, a retry outcome table, a rotation procedure that works whichever secret Orbit signs with, and a nine-row troubleshooting table. It is the only guide that reasons correctly about timestamp freshness: retries can arrive about 15 hours late and replays 7 days late, so it says to log timestamp age rather than reject on it. Its one overreach is the header table, which states under Guarantee that retries reuse the event ID; the notes say that only for replays, and A raises it only in RESPONSE.md.
strengths: The verifier takes a list of secrets, uses .get() with defaults, compares bytes in constant time, and handled every edge case I tested: missing headers, a non-ASCII signature, a garbage timestamp, and a previous secret during rotation.
Timestamp freshness is left unconfirmed, with a clear reason not to set a short window (a rejected delivery gets a non-retried 4xx).
It points out that X-Orbit-Event is not signed, which follows directly from the signing scheme.
The Unconfirmed list covers the retry interval basis, Retry-After, what happens after the last retry, redirects, which secret signs during the overlap, and timestamp semantics.
Its dedupe advice is to record an ID only after processing succeeds, and to clear the record before a deliberate replay.
weaknesses: The header table says 'Retries and manual replays of an event reuse it' under Guarantee; the notes state this only for replays.
At 1,094 words by wc -w it is right at the upper limit.
The 'Record an ID only after processing succeeds' advice does not address concurrent duplicate deliveries (no atomic claim).
evidence: '<X-Orbit-Timestamp value> + "." + <raw request body bytes>' matches the notes' 'signs timestamp + dot + raw body'; the callout calls the parsed-JSON docs 'out of date', as the notes ask ('Need state that old note conflicts').

'Retries can arrive about 15 hours after the first attempt and replays up to 7 days later ... log timestamp age instead of rejecting on it': conservative, and consistent with the notes, which give no tolerance.
'Whether each interval is measured from the previous attempt (about 14.6 h in total) or from the first attempt' flags the ambiguity in the notes' 'roughly 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 12h'.
'Redirects. Security believes they aren't followed; the implementation owner hasn't confirmed' matches the notes.
In my Python run: valid True, previous secret True, wrong secret False, re-serialized body False, missing headers False, 'v1=é' False with no exception.

muse.summary: B is readable and correctly labels guarantees and recommendations, but it states several invented details as guarantees: HTTPS delivery, the timestamp as 'send time', and replays 'for up to 7 days after its original delivery'. The code example checks a single secret, even though the guide itself says to fall back to the previous secret, and it raises exceptions on malformed input. It recommends rejecting timestamps older than 5 minutes without considering that retries and replays may keep the original timestamp. Its 'Needs product confirmation' section lists only redirects.
strengths: It clearly marks the parsed-JSON docs as stale and documents the timestamp.raw-body scheme.
Its retry and non-retry status codes are correct, and it gives useful advice on which status to return (400 to stop retries, 429/503 to get one).
It keeps User-Agent as a routing hint only, never as authentication.
weaknesses: It invents facts under Guarantee: 'an HTTPS POST', 'X-Orbit-Timestamp: send time', and replay 'for up to 7 days after its original delivery'.
It presents the retry schedule as intervals 'after the prior attempt' as if that were known, when the notes don't say.
It recommends rejecting timestamps 'older than 5 minutes'. If retries or replays keep the original timestamp, they would get a non-retried 4xx and be lost, and the guide doesn't flag this.

verify_orbit takes one secret, so the code doesn't support the rotation fallback the guide recommends. It raises TypeError on a non-ASCII signature header and UnicodeEncodeError on a non-ASCII timestamp.
The troubleshooting row 'Large payload rejected or truncated / Body exceeds the 512 KiB maximum' contradicts the guaranteed maximum, and 'fetch large objects out of band' is invented.
Uncertainty handling is thin: the open-questions section lists only redirects. Timestamp semantics, the retry interval basis and which secret signs during rotation are not flagged in the guide.
evidence: 'Guarantee: Each delivery is an HTTPS POST': the notes say only 'POST JSON'.
'X-Orbit-Timestamp: send time as Unix seconds': the notes say only 'X-Orbit-Timestamp Unix seconds'.
'reject timestamps far from your clock (for example, older than 5 minutes)' conflicts with the notes' retries up to 12h and 'replay UI can resend an event for 7 days'.

In my Python run, verify_orbit(..., 'v1=é') raised 'TypeError: comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported', and a signature from the previous secret failed because only one secret can be passed.

fable-5.1.summary: C is well organized, with a Guarantee/Recommendation/Unconfirmed legend, a good multi-step rotation procedure, retry-window arithmetic that holds under either reading ('12–15 hours'), and solid dedupe advice (atomic claim, release on failure, keep records for 8 days or more). However, its code example enforces a 300-second timestamp tolerance by default. If timestamps are not refreshed, deliveries from the second retry onward (about 6 minutes in) would be rejected with a non-retried 401 and lost. The guide flags this risk only for replays. It also invents semantics for the timestamp ('when the request was signed').
strengths: The verifier accepts a list of secrets [current, previous] and compares in constant time.
'expect the last retry 12–15 hours after the first attempt' handles the ambiguity in the schedule honestly.
It notes that a 413 from the receiver is a final 4xx and will not be retried.
The Unconfirmed section covers the signature input, redirects, the rotation signature(s), and replay timestamps.
The rotation procedure accounts for 'shown once' and the gap before deploying the new secret, with a replay step.
weaknesses: The timestamp is described as 'Unix time in seconds when the request was signed'; this meaning is invented.
The default TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300 contradicts the conservative stance the brief asks for: the risk applies to retries as well as replays, and rejected deliveries get a 401 that is never retried.
The code raises KeyError on missing headers, ValueError on a non-integer timestamp, and TypeError on a non-ASCII signature.
Some inferences are presented as guarantees: 'after that, only the current secret is valid' and 'not delivered again automatically'.
evidence: 'X-Orbit-Timestamp | Unix time in seconds when the request was signed': the notes give only 'Unix seconds'.

In my Python run, a 3-hour-old timestamp (the case where a retry keeps the original timestamp) returned False, a missing-headers input raised KeyError, 'abc' as the timestamp raised ValueError, and 'v1=é' raised TypeError.
'Replays rejected | Your timestamp tolerance ... | Widen the tolerance while replaying' covers replays but not retries.
'That description is believed stale; see Unconfirmed' is a reasonable reading of the notes' 'probably stale'.

mimo.summary: D is clear and well labeled, and it flags the signature conflict and redirects properly. The code example checks a single secret and encodes the secret as ASCII. The troubleshooting table says an event is undelivered 'after ~12 hours', which undercounts the retry span of roughly 14.6 hours if intervals are cumulative.
strengths: It has a concise, scannable structure with a separate Replay section and an Open questions list (signature input, redirects, HTTPS, schedule precision).
Its retry and non-retry codes and the 10-second 2xx rule are stated correctly.
Its advice to acknowledge unknown event types with a 2xx is useful and labeled as a Recommendation.

'over the ASCII bytes of "<X-Orbit-Timestamp>.<raw request body>"' is inaccurate, since the JSON body can contain non-ASCII bytes.
verify() takes a single secret, even though the guide recommends accepting either secret during rotation. secret.encode('ascii') and a str compare_digest raise exceptions on non-ASCII input.
It recommends rejecting timestamps 'more than a few minutes away' without considering retries and replays that may keep the original timestamp.
Rotation guidance is thin: it gives no procedure for the gap between the secret being shown once and the new secret being deployed.
evidence: 'Confirm public reachability; check Orbit's delivery log': the notes describe only a 'replay UI'.
'Event undelivered after ~12 hours | All five retries exhausted' conflicts with the notes' schedule '1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 12h', which sums to about 14.6h.
In my Python run, verify(cur, now, body, 'v1=é') raised TypeError, and a signature from the previous secret returned False because the API takes only one secret.
'Security believes redirects are not followed; the implementation owner has not confirmed' matches the notes.

sonnet-5.5.summary: E is a strong, faithful guide with a clear three-way legend, a multi-secret verifier, well-reasoned idempotency advice (atomic insert-if-absent, mark done after commit), and a ten-row troubleshooting table. It deliberately sets no timestamp freshness window, because whether the timestamp is refreshed on retries is unconfirmed. Its main flaws are that it states 'Orbit does not resend automatically' after retries run out as fact, while its own open item 6 treats that as unknown, and that its code raises KeyError on missing headers.
strengths: It names the conflict with the older docs explicitly and tells readers not to add a parsed-JSON fallback.
The ~14.5-hour retry span is marked Unconfirmed because the basis of the intervals is unknown.
Its idempotency advice covers concurrent duplicates (atomic insert) and not recording an event before processing commits.
Its open items cover redirects, key encoding, multiple signature values, which secret signs during rotation, timestamp refresh, retries reusing the event ID, and what happens after retries run out.
In my tests the verifier handled a non-ASCII signature header without crashing and accepted a signature from the previous secret.
weaknesses: 'Once they are exhausted, Orbit does not resend automatically' is stated as fact, but open item 6 lists 'What happens after the final retry fails' as unconfirmed.
The code raises KeyError when X-Orbit-Signature or X-Orbit-Timestamp is missing, and it expects bytes secrets (passing str raises TypeError).
'if you suspect compromise, contact us' names no channel.
evidence: 'Documentation from the previous system says to sign the parsed JSON. That is stale and contradicts the current implementation' matches the notes' requirement to state the conflict.
'Whether the timestamp is refreshed on retries and replays. Until then, we cannot recommend a freshness window' is conservative and not invented.
'Whether retries reuse the event ID. Replays do; retries are assumed to' distinguishes precisely what the notes state from what the guide assumes.
In my Python run, missing headers raised 'KeyError: x-orbit-signature', 'v1=é' returned False, and a signature from the previous secret returned True.
